body.value: The visual image of the specific area used as utamakura or the visual image of representative landscapes, temples and natural features in the area. These were mainly cited from illustrated guides (meisho zue) of the early modern period, such as Miyako meisho zue (An'ei 9 [1780]), Yamato meisho zue (Kansei 3 [1791]), Settsu meisho zue (Kansei 8 [1796] – Kansei 10 [1798]) etc., topographic works such as Rakuyō meisho shū (Manji 0 [1658]), Tōgoku meishōshi (Hōreki 12 [1762]) etc. and ukiyo-e prints such as the meisho-e of Utagawa Hiroshige and Katsushika Hokusai. This database complies with copyright agreements and CC licenses. Links that take you directly to the relevant pages are provided. As the National Diet Library's digital collection does not allow page by page linking, the National Institute of Japanese Literature's Shin Nihon kotenseki sōgō database was used mainly for books of classic literature. Databases of relevant museums (e.g. Tōkyō National Museum) were also included for paintings and picture scrolls (emaki).
